docs.title: Warsh is changing the Fed. Its inflation problem remains.
docs.text:
Global 
 Warsh is changing the Fed. Its inflation problem remains.
 Nicole Goodkind , Barrons 4 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:29 AM IST 
 Summary
 Warsh, as usual, declined to give forward guidance on whether the central bank is likely to further raise interest rates. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged Wednesday, but Chair Kevin Warsh had plenty of other changes in mind.
 Warsh announced plans to overhaul the central bank’s meeting schedule, reducing the number of times policymakers formally vote on interest rates each year and setting aside more time for broader discussions about monetary policy.
 Nearly half a year into his tenure, Warsh is beginning to put his stamp on the institution. But while his plans for how the Fed should operate are coming into focus, Wednesday’s press conference offered little clarity about what would persuade policymakers to raise interest rates again.
 The Fed held its benchmark rate steady between 3.75% and 4%, leaving open the possibility of another quarter-point increase at its final meeting of the year in December.
 Asked why policymakers would wait until then if another rate increase was warranted, Warsh pointed to the need for more economic information.
 He described the coming weeks as an “information rich” period, suggesting that policymakers would have a better understanding of the economy by December. What he didn’t explain was which developments in particular might change their minds.
 The Fed will receive additional readings on inflation, employment and economic activity before its next meeting, as it does ahead of most policy decisions. But the case for waiting is complicated by the central bank’s own assessment of the economy.
 Policymakers described economic activity as continuing to expand at a solid pace, even as inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target. Those conditions could give the central bank room to raise rates further without jeopardizing growth.
 Warsh has made clear his dislike of forward guidance, the practice of signaling future interest-rate decisions to financial markets. But there is a difference between declining to commit to a future decision and explaining what would justify one.
 “The press conference was tough on inflation in words but soft on action. Warsh’s refusal to give forward guidance risks being self-defeating: The market-driven restraint he’s counting on eased as the front end rallied,” said Ali Hassan of Thornburg Investment Management.
 Warsh suggested that the Fed’s earlier tightening may already be having its intended effect; mortgage rates and other interest rates have risen in recent months. Higher interest rates can slow borrowing, spending and investment, easing pressure on prices.
 “The overwhelming judgment is that what we’ve done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some, but there’s no firm conclusions,” Warsh said.
 He also suggested that interest rates may already be at an appropriate level.
 That leaves policymakers with two interpretations of the same economic conditions. If higher rates are beginning to slow the economy, the Fed may have reason to hold steady and allow the effects of its previous moves to build. But if growth remains strong and inflation stubbornly elevated, there may be room for further tightening.
 Warsh, meanwhile, is moving ahead with a grand rethinking of how the central bank makes decisions.
 Beginning in 2027, the Fed will reduce its number of scheduled voting meetings from eight to seven, reserving one meeting for broader discussions of monetary strategy without a policy vote. By 2028, it plans to hold six voting meetings and two devoted to strategy.
 “Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals,” Warsh said Wednesday.
 The announcement follows the creation of five task forces charged with examining how the Fed evaluates the economy and conducts monetary policy. Their first reports are due by the end of the year, although Warsh acknowledged Wednesday that some may miss that deadline.
 “I think some, but not all of the groups will probably hit their deadline and turn their homework in on time,” he said. “But that just begins the process.”
 Warsh said the findings would bear fruit in a future policy debate and were “unlikely to find their way into this policy conjuncture.”
 By December, the Fed will have another round of economic data and updated projections of where officials expect interest rates to go. Whether that information will be enough to justify another increase remains uncertain.
 Warsh is laying out a plan to change how the Fed makes future decisions. Wednesday offered less insight into how it will make the next one.

docs.title: The unequal geography of India's economic activity—and how to address it
docs.text:
Opinion 
 The unequal geography of India's economic activity—and how to address it
 Sudipto Mundle 4 min read 29 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Strong market forces indicate the asymmetry will stay and lead to migration to developed states. Urban local bodies must be empowered to absorb their flows. While the Finance Commissions can’t fund local bodies directly, they can incentivize states to work on preventing economic concentration. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 There are breathtaking differences in the scale of economic activity across and within the states of India, and policymakers need to address this unequal geography. 
 Among the major states, the two richest, Goa and Gujarat, have per capita incomes 10 times and six times that of Bihar, respectively. The top ranked five states account for as much as 50% of India’s total gross domestic product (GDP) while the bottom five account for only about 10%. 
 In exports, the top ranked three states—Gujarat, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu—account for 55% of total exports. The 10 states ranked at the bottom account for less than half-a-percent each. 
 In investment projects, just three states —Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka—account for over 41% of the total number of projects. The same three states, along with Tamil Nadu, also account for over 62% of total bank credit and 52% of bank deposits. 
 At the opposite end, each of the lowest-ranked 10 states accounts for less than 1% of total bank credit and seven of them have less than 1% of bank deposits. 
 This sharp concentration of economic activity is also visible at a more granular level when comparing districts within states. Among the better-off states, the district of Bengaluru Urban alone accounts for 40% of Karnataka’s gross state domestic product (GSDP). In Telangana, just two districts—Rangareddy and Hyderabad Metropolitan district—account for 35% of the state’s GSDP. 
 Similarly, Mumbai and Thane together account for 35% of the GSDP of Maharashtra. Among the poorer states, just three districts in Uttar Pradesh—Gautam Buddha Nagar, Lucknow and Ghaziabad—together account for nearly a quarter of the state’s total GSDP. In Rajasthan, Jaipur alone accounts for 15% of GSDP. 
 In exports , while Gujarat accounts for 77% of total petroleum exports, Jamnagar district accounts for 67%. The world’s largest refinery, owned by Reliance Industries, is located there. 
 In electronics, Tamil Nadu accounts for 42% of total exports while the single district of Kanchipuram accounts for 35%. In gems and jewellery exports, Maharashtra accounts for 46% of total exports while the Mumbai Suburban district alone accounts for 38%. 
 Investment projects also demonstrate extreme concentration. Of the districts currently having investment projects, 115 of them have only one project in 2025-26. Districts having 1-10 projects, the norm, account for 86% of all investment projects. But at the top-end, Mumbai alone has 152 projects, Pune has 127, Bengaluru 87 and Bharuch and Dhar 81 each. Credit flows are similarly concentrated. 
 Paul Krugman won the Nobel prize for his new theory of economic geography, that competitive market forces would lead to spatial concentration of economic activity, or divergence rather than convergence across regions. The evidence presented demonstrates how this market-driven process of spatial concentration of economic activity is powerfully at work in India. 
 Much of the wealth and income inequality in the country stems from this unequal geography of economic activity. Since market forces are driving this rising inequality across space, public policy needs to “lean against the wind” and reverse or contain such rising spatial inequality. What policy instruments do we have to deploy such a strategy? 
 The flow of bank credit, bank deposits, state government revenues and expenditure are all highly correlated with the spatial distribution of economic activity. Conventional monetary or fiscal policy instruments, thus, tend to reinforce rather than contain concentration. 
 Here, the role of the Finance Commissions is important. The Constitution mandates the Finance Commission to address the horizontal imbalance across states, and Finance Commission awards have indeed had an equalizing effect. However, this impact has been very limited compared to the strong impact of market forces in the opposite direction. 
 Thus, it is likely that the concentration of economic activity will persist, divergence between the advanced and less-developed states will increase and there will be a growing flow of workers from the less-developed states to the advanced. Many village studies confirm this. 
 Urban local governments in the advanced states need to be adequately empowered and resourced to create the infrastructure to absorb such migration: housing, water supply and sanitation, power supply, public transport and communications. 
 There is a sharp contrast here between India and China. The provincial governments in China are not as important as the urban local governments, which are very powerful bodies, raise their own resources and are highly competitive with one another in order to attract private investment. 
 In India, in contrast, a conflict of interest in power sharing between elected legislators of state governments and local bodies has left the latter with very little power and weak capacity. 
 Constitutionally, the Finance Commissions cannot directly assist local governments. However, the horizontal devolution formula can be used, with adequate weights, wherein the states are incentivized to contain the concentration of economic activity within their territories by empowering the local governments. 
 The author is chairman, Centre for Development Studies.

 AI is changing religion and religions are trying to change AI
 The Economist 7 min read 29 Oct 2026, 01:49 PM IST 
 Summary
 Will chatbots supplant the advice of imams and priests or help them spread the word? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 “WE HOPE POPE LEO will see us as his soldiers,” says Matthew Harvey Sanders, the boss of Longbeard, a Catholic startup. In a room near the Pontifical Gregorian University in Rome, the firm’s robots scan ancient books, manuscripts and codices. Scholars have long struggled to make accessible much of the “great wisdom sitting on shelves” of Catholic institutions, he says, but advances in AI mean “we can now understand the insights” of even the most worn, ancient texts. His firm then feeds this corpus into a more modern form of religious communication: Magisterium AI, a chatbot that draws on a curated library of Catholic doctrine and scholarship. According to Mr Sanders, it has millions of users across 190 countries, who use it to get “answers to profound questions”.
 Longbeard’s work shows how the world’s most cutting-edge technology is changing its oldest traditions. It also illuminates religious institutions’ and firms’ scramble to influence how AI is being developed and used. The technology is beginning to perform tasks that religions have carried out for millennia: shaping people’s outlook on life and helping them find meaning in it. The leading models are being developed by labs in Silicon Valley and China, without much religious input, which worries religious leaders. Pope Leo XIV argued in his first encyclical in May that technology is never neutral and takes on “characteristics of those who devise, finance, regulate and use it”. The fear is that AI will be unduly secular, and will undermine or even supplant religious beliefs.
 AI is changing religion in ways that many of the pious find troubling. Some are mundane, such as clerics’ growing use of it to prepare sermons and instruction. The Mormon church discourages sermons written by AI because “People ought to use their own feeling and inspiration,” says Gerrit Gong, one of its leaders. Wrestling with original texts, rather than AI summaries of them, is essential to the practice of Judaism, among other faiths. And homilies that rely on AI may include hallucinations such as misquoted scripture.
 A bigger concern is that AI may change the relationship between clergy and laity. The printing press put the Bible in the hands of many more Christians, fostering new interpretations of the faith, and then helped disseminate those views despite clerical objections. In a similar vein, the religious counsel provided by AI may diminish the importance of that provided by spiritual leaders. Waleed Kadous, who has developed Ansari, an AI chatbot for Muslims, worries that, because models are often “sycophantic and focus on the user, not their community”, believers may drift towards “more individualised” practice.
 At the extreme, AI is fuelling “religious improvisation”, says Beth Singler of the University of Zurich. As people interact more intensely with chatbots and with like-minded soul-searchers, some are forming loosely organised new faiths. For example, “Theta Noir”, a “spiritual collective”, awaits MENA, a future superintelligence with God-like powers which will bestow on humanity “the great upgrade”.
 Perhaps religious leaders’ biggest worry about AI is that many people are turning to it rather than to spiritual authorities for answers. Shaza Nasheha, a 37-year-old Muslim from Singapore, says she often asks ChatGPT to explain Islamic concepts. Religious queries accounted for roughly 5% of the total in a publicly released data set of millions of conversations with AI chatbots, according to CEFE AI, a research initiative involving several faith-based universities.
 Pastoral, but godless
 Yet these frontier models have a secular bias. A recent analysis by The Economist found that OpenAI’s models were more secular than respondents in any country on Earth (see chart). CEFE AI has put 150 questions about grief, relationships, morality and other personal or ethical problems to 27 large language models. In a forthcoming paper it describes how they invoke religion in only 5-16% of answers, even though people it surveyed averred that religious ideas would be relevant in 45-59% of cases.
 Users who ask AI for help because life feels meaningless, for example, may be directed to self-help rather than to an imam, priest or rabbi. “If companies assume secularism as defaults, there will be a weakening of faith,” says David Wingate of CEFE AI. Some religions may also be getting a rawer deal than others: in another forthcoming study, CEFE AI finds that chatbots are keener on people becoming Catholics than Jehovah’s Witnesses.
 Religious leaders fear that secular AI chatbots will not only weaken people’s faith, but also create weaker people. AI chatbots “are optimised for short-term comfort”, says Audrey Tang, a former Taiwanese government minister. Many faiths view friction, criticism and human interaction as important parts of becoming a good person. In Daoism, for example, tension between opposites is part of creation. Juewei Shi, a Buddhist nun from the Fougangshan order, worries that people won’t be able to cope with suffering—or other, flawed people—if they are used to “getting artificial comfort”. Steven Croft, a retired Anglican bishop, says, “If the whole world is seduced by narcissistic chatbots, that could make it even harder for us.”
 These concerns explain why religious groups are trying both to shape AI models and influence how believers use them. Religious AI companies are developing “harnesses” that keep chatbots “theologically aligned” by introducing guardrails and monitoring content, says Nick Skytland of Gloo, a firm that makes them.
 Most significant, though, are religious groups’ effort

docs.text:
Global 
 See the Trump administration stock portfolio that spans more than 40 companies
 David Uberti , The Wall Street Journal 3 min read 29 Oct 2026, 01:34 PM IST 
 Summary
 A $30 billion spending spree is slated to give the government stakes in chip firms, miners and more. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A slew of quantum-computing investments. A 35% stake in a firm vying for Venezuelan oil. Four equity deals in semiconductors and energy announced last week.
 The Trump administration is snapping up stakes in private companies at an unprecedented pace. Since the start of President Trump’s second term, the U.S. government has announced 43 deals involving stock ownership or warrants that may be swapped for equity at a later date.
 The spending spree has totaled around $30 billion, according to the Council on Foreign Relations. And thanks largely to a surge in the stock price in Intel, the chip maker that sold a 9.9% stake to the government in August 2025, America’s stock portfolio is sitting on gains of tens of billions of dollars.
 Many of the financial bets also include loans and supply agreements, often employing bespoke structures that analysts say have untested legal authority. While some deals extend longstanding backing of international projects through the International Development Finance Corporation, the increasingly hands-on approach has drawn criticism from free-market proponents of government overreach.
 For analysts and investors interested in Washington bolstering artificial intelligence, minerals and other industries key to America’s global clout, the holdings represent a portfolio that must be managed like any other.
 “That means tracking performance, rebalancing when needed, and optimizing returns, which shouldn’t be measured in dollars alone,” said Jonathan Hillman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. “The challenge is there are many dealmakers and no chief investment officer for Washington’s growing portfolio.”
 Here’s how the deals break down:
 Chips
 Semiconductors are the building blocks of the AI race. Of the government’s 14 announced deals in the sector, its $8.9 billion equity investment in Intel is by far the largest. A monthslong rally in the American chip-making giant’s shares pushed the market value of those holdings to as high as $61 billion, but a sharp selloff in recent weeks dragged the government’s stake to roughly $41 billion.
 In December, the government announced a preliminary agreement to invest in xLight, a laser maker whose products support chip-making, worth $150 million. In exchange, the Commerce Department agreed to give government incentives. The deal was finalized in June.
 Last week, Commerce announced equity deals totaling $389 million in funding for four chip companies: Helion, Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Vertical Semiconductor and Sibelco.
 Materials
 The U.S. has struck at least 16 deals with companies in metals, critical minerals and natural resources, key suppliers for everything from batteries to defense technology.
 Eight of these agreements include loans. Vulcan Elements and ReElement Technologies, whose products include purified materials needed for magnets, received Defense Department loans of $620 million and $80 million, respectively.
 Among the largest deals is a $2.15 billion investment from the Defense Department, alongside private investors, in Korea Zinc. The deal stemmed from U.S. and South Korean concerns that China—a mining and critical-minerals superpower—could restrict the countries’ access to important materials.
 Quantum
 The Trump administration has taken an interest in the nascent field of quantum computing, which has the potential to upend cybersecurity and turbocharge scientific research. The government has announced equity stakes in nine companies, with eight deals totaling at least $100 million of investment apiece, though most have yet to close.
 In June, Trump signed a pair of executive orders calling for the development of a quantum computer, a bid to bolster digital defenses and transition the federal government to quantum-resistant security measures.
 The largest of the government’s deals was a $1 billion commitment to IBM. The tech stalwart plans to spend an additional billion dollars of its own cash to create the first quantum-chip-making facility in the country.

docs.title: Godzilla El Niño: India must do all it can to prepare rural India for it
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Godzilla El Niño: India must do all it can to prepare rural India for it
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 29 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The government should work with states to chalk out a drought management and relief plan as this weather phenomenon gets worse. It is set to not only stokes prices but also hurt rural incomes. Here some measures policymakers should consider taking. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The El Niño in the Pacific is literally off-the-charts and may gain “unprecedented” strength by December, the World Meteorological Organization warned in an update last week. It simply means the world is entering uncharted territory. By now, it’s almost certain that the 2026-27 El Niño will be the strongest ever, surpassing past extreme weather events seen in 2015-16, and way back in 1877-78 when millions perished in India and China. 
 The ongoing El Niño’s first casualty was the south-west monsoon, which recorded a deficit of 13%, the widest since 2015. 
 The impacts are already being felt in crops such as rice, sugarcane, maize and pulses. Prices of these crops are already rising. A bigger worry is the impact this ‘Godzilla’ El Niño may have on the winter crop season beginning next month. A warmer winter and early onset of a hottest-ever summer in 2027 can singe the wheat crop. 
 As the El Niño peaks by December, parts of India may see crippling water shortages by February-March next year, or even earlier. Cities such as Hyderabad, Mumbai and Pune are already witnessing water shortages. Both the crop and non-crop farm sector (including livestock, dairy and poultry) could be hit hard as feed, fodder and water shortages intensify. 
 Agricultural economist and former Niti Aayog member Ramesh Chand has warned that farm sector growth may be close to zero or even turn negative in 2026-27. The agricultural growth rate was already losing steam, with growth at 3% in 2025-26, compared to 4.2% in the year-ago period. 
 Farm and non-farm wage growth have also been sluggish over the past year, as Mint columnist Himanshu pointed out recently. Real (inflation-adjusted) farm wages fell by 1.9% in August compared to the year-ago period while non-farm wages declined 2.1% over the same period, his estimates show. 
 This means that rural incomes are already stressed, and the super El Niño would add to that stress. 
 A small farmer in India is also a consumer purchasing multiple food items from the market. She is also a day wage earner. So, as food inflation increases, families in rural India will be pushed to spend more on essentials, impacting discretionary spending on fast moving consumer goods as well as durables. Rural demand is likely to be hit hard. 
 At a time of rising bond yields and fiscal stress, it is important for the Union government to set aside adequate funds for rural relief in the coming months. 
 One may recall that the state of Maharashtra was the first to launch a rural employment guarantee scheme following a crippling drought in 1972. It inspired the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in 2005. Funds for the revamped version of that scheme—the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin)—should be hiked to help ease rural distress. 
 The rural development ministry should ensure that enough person-days of work are generated and that families work for the full 125 days promised under the scheme. Insurance companies should be nudged to hasten crop damage assessments and pay-outs. 
 Karnataka, Maharashtra and Telangana have already announced a drought. The Union government should work with states to chalk out a drought management and relief plan. From water to wages, there’s a lot to fix in the coming months.

 The Mint Editorial Board is a panel of editorial writers with expertise across diverse domains of relevance to the newspaper’s opinion readers. The Board draws on long years of experience in business, financial and economic journalism, apart from other professional fields, although each member’s record of coverage, analysis and commentary would reveal far broader interests. This panel keeps itself in tune with the news as it unfolds and aims to reflect Mint’s views, but cannot claim a daily consensus on every issue of debate that matters. 
As a matter of routine, the Mint Editorial Board produces the newspaper’s Quick Edit, a snappy daily comment on pressing issues, and Our View, a full-length editorial on an issue that demands urgent attention. docs.title: Experts red-flag cancer drug price cuts as patented therapies see zero relief, markups exceed benchmark
docs.text:
News 
 Experts red-flag cancer drug price cuts as patented therapies see zero relief, markups exceed benchmark
 Priyanka Sharma 4 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:46 PM IST 
 Summary
 Experts said there should be comprehensive, cost-based price controls covering all oncology therapies, permanent statutory margin caps across distribution channels and full scrutiny of company assistance programmes. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: India’s healthcare industry and public health experts have warned that price cuts of non-scheduled cancer medicines effective 9 November under the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s trade margin rationalization exercise are structurally flawed, legitimize profiteering and completely bypass high-cost patented drugs. 
 One-off, self-reported price revisions without independent verification will fail to deliver lasting relief, health groups said, demanding comprehensive, cost-based price controls covering all oncology therapies, permanent statutory margin caps across distribution channels and full scrutiny of company assistance programmes. 
 They also urged the government to mandate supply-chain data audits and expand public cancer care infrastructure to ensure access is determined by medical need rather than commercial pricing. 
 “We welcome the government’s move to cap trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs. However, the real test is whether patients benefit, without loopholes undermining the intended relief,” said Jyotsna Govil, chairperson of the Indian Cancer Society in New Delhi. 
 According to public health network Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India, the government's policy formula legitimizes an excessive 42.8% markup over the stockist price in supply chains involving direct hospital sales. This is much higher than the 16% retail margin under the Drug Price Control Order. 
 Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India noted that while prices of generic brands fell sharply—such as Palbociclib (Palbopro 125 mg) crashing from ₹ 40,421 to ₹ 2,720 and Thiotepa (Samtepa 100 mg) plunging from ₹ 80,072 to ₹ 7,150—the policy formula legitimizes high distributor markups instead of mandating cost-based price control. 
 “The dramatic collapse in cancer drug prices exposes the staggering exploitation of patients over the years by pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian generic manufacturers that offered inflated trade margins while families faced unaffordable treatment costs,” said Amulya Nidhi, national co-convenor of Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India. “Controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving treatment must be affordable and based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.”
 Prices unchanged 
 An evaluation of the 24-page NPPA compliance notification and document shows that high-cost patented therapies and imported innovator brands remained completely untouched because medicines supplied free under patient assistance programmes were excluded from calculations. 
 Consequently, there was no price reduction for several exorbitantly priced patented therapies. Prices remained unchanged for AstraZeneca ’s lung cancer therapy Osimertinib and Selumetinib, MSD’s Pembrolizumab, Roche’s breast cancer combo Phesgo, Alecensa and Avastin, Janssen’s Daratumumab, Astellas’s Gilteritinib and Padcev, Johnson & Johnson’s Rybrevant, Takeda’s Alunbrig, GSK’s Jemperli, Pfizer’s Lorbriqua and AbbVie’s Imbruvica.
 “While a detailed examination is required, the prices of many original manufacturers appear to have remained unchanged. My only worry remains that the low-cost, life-saving drug should remain viable to manufacture and sell. In the past we have seen that getting affected because of price control,” said Dr. Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital in Bengaluru. “The primary impact is likely to be on drugs that have traditionally been marketed with very high profit margins. Overall, the move appears reasonable, with its long-term impact depending on how effectively it is implemented.” 
 Medical professionals stressed that access to newer therapies remains critical. 
 “We need to ensure that newer therapies and innovative medicines are also accessible, alongside transparent pricing and effective implementation. Ultimately, no patient should have to compromise on treatment because of cost,” said Dr. Aashish Chaudhry, managing director of Aakash Healthcare. 
 The pricing directive comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court, responding to public interest litigations challenging exorbitant markups, criticizing the vast gap between wholesale procurement rates and printed retail prices. It cited instances where an injection procured at ₹ 11,000 was billed to hospital patients at ₹ 1.3 lakh. The court asked why margin caps were selectively applied to non-scheduled cancer medicines rather than across all essential drugs. 
 Cancer drug market 
 India's anti-cancer market comprises roughly 225 drugs and 500 formulations, generating an annual turnover of ₹ 12,500 crore. Scheduled medicines covering 63 drugs under the National List of Essential Medicines 2022 accounted for about ₹ 2,250 crore under statutory ceiling prices, leaving over ₹ 10,250 crore non-scheduled, where uncurbed margins drive up out-of-pocket spending.
 According to Govil of the Indian Cancer Society, the government’s projected annual savings are encouraging, but these must translate into measurable reductions in patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure. 
 “Too often, such initiatives lose their effectiveness due to inadequate monitoring and weak implementation. Regular compliance reviews, accessible grievance redressal and transparent reporting are essential,” Govil said. “Patients and patient support groups must be consulted on policy design and implementation. Affordable cancer care must also strengthen organizations providing financial, emotional and practical sup

docs.title: A green giant’s pollution woes: How Waaree Energies dumped toxic effluents in a Gujarat village
docs.text:
Long Story 
 A green giant’s pollution woes: How Waaree Energies dumped toxic effluents in a Gujarat village
 Nehal Chaliawala 12 min read 29 Oct 2026, 09:06 PM IST 
 Summary
 India’s solar poster child built a ₹ 1-trillion valuation on promises of a cleaner future. But along a quiet Gujarat stream, villagers point to foul runoff—and government records reveal repeated pollution notices. A Mint investigation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Retired army man Satish Patel, 50, laments that water from the rivulet running behind his home is no longer fit for consumption, even for cattle. When he was a child, his family directly used water from the barely 10-foot-wide stream that has no official name but is locally called Chanandevi. 
 Today, the water has changed colour. “During the monsoon, when fish reach here from upstream, they die,” he says. 
 Patel blames pollution from the massive solar cell and module manufacturing plant across the stream from his house. Operated by Waaree Energies Ltd. , the poster child of India’s clean energy push, the factory has been releasing untreated industrial water right into Chanandevi, Patel alleges.
 The stream cuts through Sunthwad village in Chikhli taluka of Navsari, in the agricultural belt of South Gujarat. Just outside the village, it merges into the Vanganiya river, a tributary of the Ambika river. 
 When Mint visited Patel’s home on a warm Sunday morning earlier this month, a foul smell permeated the air in the mango orchard behind his house. Deeper in the orchard, away from the house and towards the stream, the odour grew stronger. Two concrete pipes, each about two feet wide, were releasing a steady trickle of water into the Chanandevi. A white substance coats the algae where this runoff meets the rivulet. 
 “It’s a trickle right now, but at night, they dump a lot of water,” Patel says. 
 Mint could not verify if the discharge increases under the cover of darkness. However, an investigation by this publication found that the Chikhli factory of Waaree Energies was repeatedly pulled up by a government watchdog for violating pollution norms, including for releasing highly acidic wastewater straight into the stream. 
 The Chikhli factory is Waaree Energies’ only operational integrated solar cell and module factory, as well as one of India’s largest integrated solar module manufacturing units, with 5.4 gigawatts of annual capacity. It started assembling solar panels from imported cells in 2022. 
 Three years later, the factory started the much more complex job of producing the cells, a process that requires a number of toxic chemicals and generates effluents. Waaree Energies has a second solar cell plant with 10-gigawatt capacity coming up in neighbouring Unn, just about 20 kilometers away. 
 The Chikhli factory effluent issue has repercussions far beyond the village of Sunthwad or the boardroom of Waaree Energies. It raises questions on how ready the country is to responsibly manage the ongoing policy-driven surge in solar cell manufacturing and, eventually, chip making. Could energy sustainability come at the cost of water pollution? 
 Six warnings
 Between April 2025 and August 2026, the Waaree factory received six notices from the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB), a regulator, for repeated environmental infractions, according to documents accessed by Mint under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The violations ranged from mishandling of chemicals and ponding of acidic wastewater within the factory premises to outright release of effluents into the rivulet.
 In its first notice of directions sent to the company on 21 April 2025, the GPCB noted that the company was releasing wastewater from the storm water drainage—the two concrete pipes mentioned above—into the stream behind the factory. A notice of direction is a binding order. It landed less than a month after the factory’s solar cell manufacturing unit was inaugurated by the state’s chief minister Bhupendra Patel and the union minister of new and renewable energy Pralhad Joshi.
 The second notice followed three months later, in July 2025. This time, the factory’s effluent treatment plant, mechanical vapour recompression evaporator, and agitated thin film dryer were non-operational, the regulator found during an inspection. These systems are meant to treat the effluents from the solar cell manufacturing process so that there is zero liquid discharge.
 The factory was also sourcing water tankers, which it was not permitted to do—it is only permitted to use water from borewells and a canal.
 When the regulators inspected the factory a month later, it hadn’t yet complied with the directions of the July 2025 notice, leading to a third notice of directions in August 2025.
 The notices directed the factory to comply with all the necessary regulations, failing which the regulator warned that it will order a shutdown. And that is what happened five months later, when during an inspection in January 2026, Waaree Energies was again found to be releasing wastewater into the Chanandevi. The wastewater had a pH reading of 2-4, according to GPCB’s closure direction to Waaree. That is a strongly acidic level, comparable to the stomach acid of humans.
 Moreover, the GPCB inspectors found that a pond of similar acidic wastewater, as expansive as six tennis courts, had accumulated within the factory premises. The mechanical vapour recompression evaporator and the agitated thin film dryer were still non-operational.
 A fourth notice to the company on 28 January ordered it to shut the Chikhli factory within 15 days. The regulator directed the local power distribution company to cut its power supply, documents show.
 Corrective action
 Waaree Energies took prompt corrective action. During a follow-up inspection on 4 February, GPCB noted that the storm water drainage pipes dumping water into the stream

docs.title: Selling a house to clear your home loan? What an ITAT ruling on a ₹26 lakh cash advance means for property sellers
docs.text:
In its order dated 13 October 2026 in Murugesan Thulasimani v. ITO, Ward-1(6), Salem (ITA No. 859/Chny/2026), the tribunal held that the penalty under Section 271D of the Income-tax Act, 1961, was not sustainable after considering the taxpayer's outstanding housing loan, the genuineness of the property sale and the circumstances in which he accepted the cash. The ruling does not exempt cash property transactions from tax law. Instead, it highlights how the circumstances of an individual transaction can determine whether a penalty is justified. Thulasimani, a salaried employee with an annual income of ₹ 3.41 lakh for assessment year 2017-18, had an outstanding housing loan of ₹ 25.38 lakh from Axis Bank. According to the tribunal's order, he had been trying to sell his residential property for several months to repay the loan. On 24 November 2016, he entered into an unregistered sale agreement with a buyer and accepted an advance of ₹ 26 lakh in cash. The property sale was subsequently completed on 6 February 2017. During the demonetisation period, the taxpayer deposited ₹ 24.13 lakh in cash into his bank account. The assessing officer questioned the source of the deposit and did not accept the explanation, although the sale transaction was confirmed by the seller and the buyer's representative during the proceedings. The tax department subsequently imposed a ₹ 26 lakh penalty under Section 271D for violating Section 269SS, which restricts the acceptance of specified sums relating to the transfer of immovable property through cash rather than prescribed banking channels. The taxpayer challenged the penalty, but the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, upheld it on 31 January 2026. He then appealed to the tribunal. The tribunal examined whether the taxpayer had established reasonable cause under Section 273B, which provides relief from certain penalties where the taxpayer demonstrates reasonable cause for the failure to comply with the law. It noted that the property transaction was genuine, had been confirmed by the parties and was subsequently completed. The outstanding housing loan and the taxpayer's efforts to sell the property to discharge the liability were also relevant considerations. The tribunal observed that the tax department had not produced evidence showing that the transaction was fictitious, that the taxpayer's explanation about the loan was false, or that the transaction was designed to introduce undisclosed money or evade tax. Considering these circumstances together, the bench concluded that the taxpayer had demonstrated a bona fide financial exigency and reasonable cause for accepting the advance in cash. It set aside the appellate order and directed the assessing officer to delete the ₹ 26 lakh penalty. Section 269SS covers specified sums received in connection with the transfer of immovable property, including advances, even when the transfer has not yet taken place. A genuine transaction, therefore, does not automatically remove the requirement to follow the prescribed payment methods. The ruling instead demonstrates the importance of Section 273B. The tribunal considered the taxpayer's financial position, outstanding loan, supporting evidence and the subsequent completion of the sale before granting relief. Property sellers should continue to use banking channels for advances and sale consideration and retain sale agreements, payment records and loan documents. If a cash transaction has already taken place, the outcome will depend on its specific facts and the evidence available. The decision is a fact-specific ruling, not a blanket permission to accept cash for property transactions. Kirti Jha is a Senior Content Producer at Mint, where she writes on mutual funds, taxation, personal finance and macroeconomic developments. Her reporting focuses on helping readers understand complex financial developments through data-driven, research-backed stories that explain how policy changes, market trends and regulatory decisions affect investors and households.

Before joining Mint, Kirti worked at ET Money, where she specialised in mutual fund research and investment analysis. She tracked portfolio disclosures, fund manager strategies, sectoral allocation shifts and investment trends, distilling large datasets into investor-focused insights. Her work combined quantitative analysis with consumer-centric storytelling, enabling readers to better understand fund positioning, portfolio changes and long-term investment opportunities.

Kirti holds a Bachelor's degree in Economics from Indraprastha College for Women, University of Delhi, and a Master's in Finance from the Jindal School of Banking & Finance at O.P. Jindal Global University. Her academic training emphasised analytical thinking, quantitative research and financial decision-making, providing a strong foundation in understanding capital markets, financial systems and economic policy. docs.title: How Bolsonaro fled Brazil: decoys, a private jet and a friend in the White House
docs.text:

 How Bolsonaro fled Brazil: decoys, a private jet and a friend in the White House
 Vera Bergengruen , Samantha Pearson , Ryan Dubé , Philip Wegmann , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:57 AM IST 
 Summary
 After losing Brazil’s election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in an elaborate operation aided by Trump’s inner circle and Argentina’s president, Javier Milei. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Less than 24 hours after losing Brazil’s presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro appeared to vanish into a convoy of four dark cars.
 After pulling away from his home in Brasília on Monday evening, the vehicles split in different directions, leaving journalists and authorities scrambling to determine which one carried Bolsonaro. By the next afternoon, the former presidential candidate’s allies were telling reporters he had already reached Florida.
 As Brazilian and international outlets reported that Bolsonaro had left the country, he was still in Brazil, while a private jet waited for him across the border in Argentina. At 12:21 a.m. Wednesday, the Gulfstream G400 took off from Puerto Iguazú and whisked him to Ecuador and then Miami, where his entry was facilitated by Trump allies his family spent years cultivating.
 The getaway—which relied heavily on deception and decoys—sparked a global guessing game that left even some of Bolsonaro’s closest allies in Washington and Brazil in the dark about his whereabouts.
 After Bolsonaro stepped off the plane in Miami on Wednesday morning wearing a navy polo shirt and a backpack, uniformed officers used umbrellas to shield him and his family from cameras. Their arrival followed an extraordinary effort by a small circle of influential Trump allies, senior U.S. officials and Argentine President Javier Milei to help him fly to the U.S. and secure entry, despite a Brazilian court order barring Bolsonaro from leaving the country.
 Referring to himself as the “leader of Brazil,” Bolsonaro thanked President Trump for welcoming him to a “land of freedoms” and Milei for his “courage” and “sense of justice” in a statement from Miami Wednesday.
 After Trump personally approved admitting Bolsonaro and his family to the U.S. on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved to issue them visas, according to people familiar with the arrangements. But the family entered the country under humanitarian parole, which allows them to remain for one year, the people said.
 The operation to whisk Bolsonaro out of Brazil to the U.S. took shape on Monday, as allies grew concerned that he could face arrest. Although the criminal investigations into Bolsonaro predated the election, the Supreme Court order barring him from leaving Brazil and requiring him to surrender his passports came shortly after his defeat and fueled accusations that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was determined to punish his political rival.
 Working with Flávio Bolsonaro’s well-connected younger brother Eduardo, a small group including Trump adviser Jason Miller secured a charter jet to take him from Argentina to Florida.
 The Trump administration’s decision to provide refuge to Bolsonaro marks the culmination of the family’s yearslong lobbying campaign to enlist the U.S. president and his inner circle in its legal and political battles at home. The personal alliance between the two most powerful political families in the hemisphere has reshaped relations between the U.S. and Brazil. Last year, Trump imposed steep tariffs on the country citing its treatment of Bolsonaro and sanctioned the same Supreme Court justice who barred Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil.
 President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term in Brazil. WSJ’s Samantha Pearson explains what Lula’s victory means for President Trump and his right-wing allies in Latin America. Photo: Paulo Lopes/Xinhua/ZUMA Press
 Now, what began as a domestic political and legal battle in Brazil is becoming a test of how far Trump is willing to wield American power on behalf of a foreign political dynasty—with potentially far-reaching consequences for the second-largest democracy in the Americas.
 Bolsonaro intends to set up a political operation in exile from the U.S., people involved in discussions with him said. But with the U.S. midterm elections days away, the White House has given little indication that it intends to go beyond offering Bolsonaro refuge or that Trump will expend political capital challenging da Silva’s re-election victory, despite pressure from allies in Washington, according to two people involved in the discussions.
 Trump declined to comment when reporters asked him about Bolsonaro declaring himself the rightful president of Brazil. “I thought they were treated very unfairly,” he said on Wednesday about the Bolsonaros, who he described as “very fine people” earlier in the day. “But I won’t get involved—it was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”
 Da Silva’s victory in Sunday’s runoff election against Bolsonaro was recognized by more than 50 countries, including Latin American leaders across the political spectrum. He defeated Bolsonaro by more than 4.4 million votes, a margin that international observers said left no doubt about the integrity of the country’s electoral data. Trump, however, has so far refused to formally recognize da Silva’s victory, instead suggesting without evidence that the results might have been rigged.
 The long way to Miami
 On Tuesday, the conservative senator and his family headed to the Argentine border, hundreds of miles away. That night, at 10:50 p.m. local time, Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters crossed the Tancredo Neves International Bridge into Puerto Iguazú, Argentina, near where the borders of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet, according to Argentine authorities.
 After crossing the border, Bolsonaro’s vehicle was escorted by Argenti

docs.title: U.S. economy set to deliver remarkably resilient third quarter growth
docs.text:
Global 
 U.S. economy set to deliver remarkably resilient third quarter growth
 Megan Leonhardt , Barrons 2 min read 29 Oct 2026, 01:43 PM IST 
 Summary
 The bulk of third-quarter GDP growth is expected to come from AI investments. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A new batch of economic data Thursday is expected to show the U.S. economy strengthened substantially over the last three months, driven by resilient consumer spending and a surge in the artificial intelligence buildout.
 The Bureau of Economic Analysis’ first estimate of third quarter gross domestic product growth will be published at 8:30 a.m. Forecasts from leading economists and Federal Reserve models vary some—but all agree that third-quarter growth dramatically beat the second quarter’s 2.2% growth rate. A rosy GDP report will be welcomed by the president and his Republican party as voters concerned about the economy head to the polls in the midterm elections next week.
 Economists surveyed by FactSet expect that GDP adjusted for inflation grew at an annualized rate of 3% in the third quarter. Bloomberg calls for a 3.2% advance.
 The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow model estimate is even higher, forecasting that growth was 3.4% in the third quarter. The New York Fed’s Staff Nowcast model, however, predicts a gain of just 2.7%.
 The bulk of the growth likely came from continued AI-related business investment growth. Business fixed investment growth is expected to have advanced by 10.2% in the third quarter, a significant acceleration from the 7.7% growth in the prior quarter.
 “The strong AI spending continues to drive business investment, and there are spillovers and strengthening capex outside of tech even amid higher borrowing rates and energy costs,” Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide, wrote in a note.
 The AI investment boom still trails the 1990s tech cycle in terms is spending, but not by much. Capital spending on AI-related goods and services has increased by roughly 1.2% of GDP since the first quarter of 2020, compared with about 1.5% during the same period within the 1990s internet boom.
 Final sales to domestic purchasers will also be in focus, Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, wrote. The metric tends to give a “cleaner read on how much Americans are buying, regardless of where the goods were made or whether they sat in a warehouse,” Pride noted.
 Trade, however, is expected to subtract from growth. The advance goods trade deficit widened to nearly $135 billion in September, its largest level since the first quarter of 2025.
 At the consumer level, growth in spending from July through September is expected to have been slightly softer than the second quarter. Goldman Sachs’ economists project that U.S. real personal consumption expenditures increased at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, compared with 3.8% in the second quarter.
 With the benefits of 2025 tax cuts fading and high fuel costs squeezing Americans, the third quarter may be the last of the resilient consumer spending gains the U.S. will see for a while, according to JPMorgan’s Bruce Kasman. He expects consumer expenditure growth to cool to 1.5% in the fourth quarter.
 Write to megan.leonhardt@barrons.com.

docs.title: The Fed held steady on rates, leaving investors to sit tight, too
docs.text:
Global 
 The Fed held steady on rates, leaving investors to sit tight, too
 Sam Goldfarb , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:59 AM IST 
 Summary
 Stocks and long-term bond yields edged higher after Wall Street read Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh as hesitant to hike aggressively. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Federal Reserve is in a holding pattern. And so are markets.
 U.S. stocks and longer-term bond yields ticked higher after the Fed held interest rates steady as expected and Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh made comments that investors interpreted as slightly dovish—indicating that the central bank likely won’t embark on a rapid series of rate increases in the coming months.
 Warsh said at Wednesday’s postmeeting press conference that financial and credit conditions had tightened since the Fed raised rates last month—a sign, he suggested, that the central bank’s policies were already starting to work by moving toward “a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”
 Stock investors were generally cheered by the tone of Warsh’s comments, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average ticking up 0.2%, or roughly 98 points, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite both rising 0.3%. Bonds were more mixed, with longer-term yield rising even as short-term yields fell—a sign of some modest concern that the Fed might be too complacent in fighting inflation.
 “All in all, I would say the market is taking this as less likelihood of aggressive hiking,” said Anders Persson, chief investment officer and head of global fixed income at Nuveen. There was, he added, “nothing scary coming out of the conversation here today.”
 Heading into Wednesday, stocks had effectively treaded water in the six weeks since the Fed’s previous meeting, with the S&P 500 inching up 0.7% over that span. That broad performance, however, masked significant turmoil beneath the surface, as investors went hot and cold on the all-important AI trade, alternatively sapping and boosting demand for stocks in other sectors.
 Worries about rising borrowing costs and the future demand for AI models have dragged on tech shares for much of October. Still, many of them rebounded this week after Anthropic unveiled long-awaited paperwork for an initial public offering, showcasing data about its revenue growth, profitability and breadth of customers. The details helped reassure investors that demand for AI tools can keep pace with companies’ outsize spending on the infrastructure needed to power them.
 Results from tech giants Alphabet and Microsoft after the market close on Wednesday were expected to shed further light on those trends. Alphabet shares fell in after-hours trading after the Google parent reported advertising revenues that fell short of expectations. Microsoft rose in late trading after the software giant reported revenue that beat Wall Street estimates.
 Many investors see the Fed as one of the biggest threats to stocks right now. Expectations that the Fed will keep raising interest rates have driven up yields on U.S. government bonds. Higher yields have, in turn, put pressure on stocks by lifting borrowing costs across the economy and boosting the appeal of Treasurys as an alternative to riskier assets.
 Stocks and bonds now appear to be in an uneasy equilibrium. After the yield on the 10-year note reached a 24-year high above 5.3% earlier this month, investors quickly started selling tech stocks and buying bonds in a flight to safety. That pulled the 10-year yield back below 5%, providing some relief to stocks. But analysts say that yields could easily rise again if tech stocks continue to rebound and inflation remains elevated—a development that could eventually undermine that rally, as it did before.
 The 10-year yield was hovering just above 5% in late-afternoon trading Wednesday, according to Tradeweb, up from 4.992% Tuesday.
 Overall, the historic spending by tech companies is a major reason why the economy is proving so resilient and why the Fed is likely to raise rates further, said Jason Granet, chief investment officer at BNY.
 At some point, rising rates will slow the economy, but it could take time to get there because “there’s no one who’s calling for a massive ratchet-up in rates,” Granet said.
 Data to be released Thursday are expected to show that the core personal expenditures price index, a favored inflation gauge of the Fed, rose a little over 3% in September from a year earlier, well above the Fed’s 2% target.
 Some investors remain optimistic that inflation can gradually fall back to 2% without further rate increases, arguing that price increases are being driven by temporary factors such as President Trump’s tariff increases and rising energy costs spurred by the U.S.-Iran conflict.
 Some Fed officials have, in fact, framed last month’s rate increase as a risk-management move: a step to guard against inflation becoming entrenched rather than the first in a series of hikes. Others, though, have argued that rates need to move high enough to actively restrain the economy, raising the prospect of a more aggressive central bank that could cause more havoc in markets.
 Two officials cast dissenting votes Wednesday in favor of raising rates by a quarter of a percentage point. That was roughly in line with Wall Street’s expectations, though some were surprised that one of the dissenters was Fed governor Lisa Cook, who had never voted against a Fed decision in the past.
 As it stands, interest rate futures suggest that the investors see a roughly 85% chance that the Fed raises rates in December and a 57% chance of three more hikes in total by the end of next year, according to CME Group data.
 Oil prices remain near their highest levels of the year, making the Fed’s job more difficult as investors brace for a possible resumption of combat operations after next week’s U.S. midterm elec

docs.title: 'Classified material missing from Epstein files': Report reveals clues, email gaps
docs.text:
What exactly was classified and why, it remains a mystery.
One of the documents shows Todd Blanche's Office of the Deputy Attorney General itself received classified material related to Epstein in March 2025, CBC News reported. By law, material can only be classified for national security purposes.
This comes despite Attorney General Blanche long maintaining that the so-called Epstein files, even those kept from the public, contain no secret information related to national security.
When the document releases began last winter, Blanche noted that the Epstein Files Transparency Act authorised withholding information in the interest of national security or foreign policy, but said, "no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis."
"There's not some tranche of super-secret documents about Jeffrey Epstein that we're withholding, we're actually not withholding anything based upon [national defense information]," Blanche, who was deputy attorney general at the time, was quoted by CBS News as saying.
The Department of Justice reportedly claimed that it collected 6 million pages of material and ultimately released over 3 million of those pages after reviewing for duplication, attorney-client privilege and relevance to Jeffrey Epstein.
Congressional challenges and a lawsuit are casting doubts on the DOJ's claims and demanding the release of more documents that were held back.
Included among the Epstein files is an eight-page timeline of the FBI's New York office's initial efforts last year to track down and deliver its voluminous files to the Justice Department's Washington headquarters.
On March 25, 2025, one document shows delivery of "16 Epstein items to ODAG," referring to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General. Among them, items No. 2 and No. 6 are described as "Epstein Transparency Project - Classified Material" and "CDs with classified materials (x2)," CBS reported.
The Epstein Transparency Project refers to the Justice Department's effort to review the files and redact, withhold or clear them for release.
It is not clear what exactly was identified as classified. Each CD was likely capable of holding hundreds of megabytes of material.
The files also contained an email sent that same day from the unit chief of the National Security Classification Operations Unit — an office whose role is to review FBI documents for classification or declassification.
The email includes an attachment labeled "Epstein - Classified Document Memo.docx."
The body of the email says there were three documents "identified that remain classified." One was described as an "FBI document which is classified when see-through." A redaction obscures the unit chief's description of the other two documents, the report claimed.
The identity of the email's recipient was also redacted.
It's also not clear whether the two documents — the email and the list — are referring to the same classified material.
A CBS News analysis of a numerical coding system used by the DOJ to organise the Epstein files offers clues about some of the documents the department has withheld.
The codes don't reveal what's missing, but they do show where gaps exist, raising questions about the DOJ's explanation for why documents were withheld.
Among the missing documents are pages from Epstein's own financial records collected as evidence in a federal prosecution.
Here's how it works: Documents from the Epstein files are labeled with a string of numbers beginning with the letters EFTA stamped on the bottom right-hand corner; EFTA stands for Epstein Files Transparency Act.
Those are called Bates numbers — a common way of organizing massive document batches in legal cases. Every page receives its own number. In the Epstein files, the sequence goes from 1 to 2,858,498, which is the tally of approximately how many pages of documents were released
According to the DOJ, other documents — including court records and investigative files they've previously released — bring the total to over 3 million.
Alongside the Epstein files' Bates numbers are other, older coding numbers that appear on many documents. This indicates that those documents had previously been used in federal legal cases, potentially collected as part of an earlier subpoena.
For instance, Bates coding on some of the documents is from the Ghislaine Maxwell criminal case and was used to organize files given to Maxwell's legal team ahead of her 2021 trial as part of the discovery process.
Other Bates numbers indicate documents were collected from Epstein's banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, during the FBI's investigation into his trafficking activities.
Similar gap analyses have been done in the past by independent researchers.
Finding gaps in these documents is a simple process of counting.
In tens of thousands of instances, the main EFTA number will advance by one but the other Bates numbers advance by two or more. Those gaps indicate pages that had been there before were likely removed at some point after the DOJ obtained them.
In another example, a series of around 4,500 images of checks from Epstein's accounts has gaps where 66 of those check images should be. Oftentimes the missing image is only the front or the back of the check, although in several cases both are missing.
Comparing all of these numbers against the final EFTA page numbers, it is possible to calculate that there are tens of thousands of pages of documents that are missing from these sections, with no clear reason why.
"Financial records were not a permissible category for removal," Barbara McQuade, the former U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, told CBS News.
Like every federal prosecutor, she says she is very familiar with Bates numbers. "It's the reason you have Bates numbers, so you notice something like that," she said.

Can Sensex, Nifty extend rally on Friday? Here's what market analysts say
 Technical analysts believe that the Sensex and Nifty can extend their rally in the near-term, with indices closing above the short-term moving averages, and positive cues from momentum indicators.
 Sensex, Nifty outlook for Friday: Market experts believe the Nifty can potentially rally to 23,200 levels in the near-term.
 Rex Cano Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 7:56 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion. Equity benchmark indices, the BSE Sensex , and the NSE Nifty 50 , rallied over 1 per cent on Thursday, supported by strong Q2 earnings and hopes of US-Iran peace talks. The Sensex closed at 74,151, and the Nifty settled at 22,937. Friday morning GIFT Nifty hinted for a likely quiet start to the market action. Market experts believe that the Sensex and Nifty can extend their rally in the near-term based on the positive developments on the technical charts. Sensex, Nifty outlook: Here's what market analysts predict.
 After a series of bearish patterns like lower tops and bottoms, the recent market action signals confirmation of a new higher bottom around 22,400 levels on the Nifty, highlights Nagaraj Shetti, Senior Technical Research Analyst at HDFC Securities. Shetti reckons that this could possibly open bullish chart formations like higher highs and lows ahead. The analyst believes that the short-term trend of Nifty remains positive, and the index may advance towards the next resistance of 23,200 in the short term. 
 Ajit Mishra, SVP – research at Religare Broking flags that technically the Nifty's move above the 20-day exponential moving average (DEMA) around 22,825 offers near-term relief and improves the prospects of an advance towards the 23,100–23,300 zone. On the downside, Mishra sees the 22,500–22,700 zones as the immediate support, while the broader 22,200–22,400 band is expected to remain an important downside reference. CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates Additionally, Om Mehra, Technical Research Analyst at SAMCO Securities notes that the Relative Strength Index (RSI) is now holding above the 50-mark for Nifty. Further, India VIX dropped 7 per cent to 15.12, slipping below 16, thus supporting the bullish move and the advance-decline ratio also improved. Mehra says that the Nifty now holds comfortably above the 20-day simple moving average (DSMA), placed around 22,700. He believes that a double bottom formation is slowly taking shape. On the upside, the index may test its next hurdle around 23,220, where the 50-DSMA is positioned, he adds. On similar lines, Sachin Gupta, VP-Technical Research at Choice Equity Broking believes that the outlook on Sensex has improved to sideways to bullish, supported by strong buying, a bullish daily candle and improving RSI momentum on Thursday. Gupta says that holding above 73,200–73,500 will be crucial for sustaining the recovery, while a move beyond 74,400–74,700 could trigger further upside. "The broader trading range stands at 73,200–74,700, with the bias shifting towards sideways to bullish. Amid near-term headwinds, Street is bullish on Hindustan Unilever
 HUL's Q2 revenue rises 15% as volume growth improves, but higher raw material costs squeeze margins; analysts see potential for a recovery in the stock
 premium 
 HUL said it strengthened distribution, adding 30,000 outlets in general trade. In modern trade, technology-led improvements enhanced service levels in ecommerce and quick commerce (Photo: Bloomberg)
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 11:20 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Hindustan Unilever Limited’s (HUL’s) July-September quarter (Q2FY27) results showed some growth, but also a degree of margin compression which may be of concern. The demerger of the ice-cream division complicated calculations.
 HUL registered consolidated revenue growth of 15 per cent (adjusted for ice-cream demerger) to ₹18,070 crore, which was the strongest year-on-year (Y-o-Y) growth in many quarters. The volume growth was 7 per cent Y-o-Y, while price hikes accounted for the rest. Volume was soft in tea and soap segments. However, a low base effect due to a flat Q2FY26 may have pushed volumes up on a Y-o-Y basis. 
 Home Care segment’s revenue grew 21 per cent Y-o-Y on double-digit underlying volume growth, but earnings before interest and taxes (Ebit) was only up 3 per cent Y-o-Y. The Ebit margin contracted 300 basis points (bps) Y-o-Y to 16 per cent, which was a multi-year low, given high raw material inflation. The Beauty & Wellbeing segment saw 16 per cent revenue growth and 16 per cent Ebit growth. Personal Care reported 8 per cent revenue growth, while Ebit dipped 9 per cent. Food & Refreshment posted 9 per cent revenue growth and 16 per cent Ebit growth.
 The gross margin dropped 400 bps Y-o-Y to 48 per cent. It was at 49.5 per cent in Q1FY27. The earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margin saw a drop of 130 bps Y-o-Y to 22.4 per cent. Absolute Ebitda grew 8 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹4,090 crore in Q2, adjusted for ice-cream demerger. HUL compensated to an extent by cutting advertising and promotional spend and other cost efficiencies. Management guidance for Ebitda margin in the medium term was 22-24 per cent.
 Concerns like high inflation, rising interest rates, deficient monsoon, etc., may be significant when it comes to consumer demand, but management commentary was positive. The stock has corrected quite substantially in 2026 so far, due to the poor growth and inflation outlook. This may attract value investors who bet on a medium-term recovery.
 Segment wise, Home Care delivered double-digit volume growth, with revenue up 21 per cent to ₹6,880 crore. Fabric Wash and Household Care delivered growth across brands and formats. Liquids sustained double-digit growth.
 Personal Care revenue grew 8 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹2,620 crore on flat volumes. Ebit declined 9 per cent Y-o-Y, while margin contracted 310 bps to 17.2 per cent. Food & Refreshment saw 9 per cent growth on like-for-like basis, after adjusting for ice-cream demerger. Segment revenue was up 9 per cent Y-o-Y at ₹3,850 crore on like-for-like basis, with low-single-digit volume growth. Lifestyle Nutrition and Packaged Foods had double-digit growth. Coffee recorded high-single-digit growth.
 Employee expenses grew 18 per cent Y-o-Y. 
 The adjusted profit after tax (PAT) was up 9 per cent at ₹2,790 crore. 
 HUL said it strengthened distribution, adding 30,000 outlets in general trade. In modern trade, technology-led improvements enhanced service levels in ecommerce and quick commerce. The Home Care segment’s margin was under pressure due to high crude linked costs and a time lag between cost inflation and hikes in pricing. In Beauty, sequential recovery may be via structural improvement, supported by brand equity, better distribution, improved in-store visibility and product innovation. Health & Wellbeing was subdued. 
 HUL saw sequential improvement in volume over the last three quarters, despite high price increases. Management said it was confident of delivering volume-led revenue and profit growth. The rural picture continued to improve sequentially, and both urban and rural markets reported positive momentum. Management has not observed significant deterioration in demand so far, despite price hikes. But it will continue to monitor inflation and the impact of the monsoon. The pricing power may be tempered by impact on demand if that is seen. Quick commerce is a structural growth opportunity for premium products targeting affluent consumers. HUL is working with platform partners to expand category penetration.
 HUL needs higher topline growth, which seems to be the focus, backed by volume growth acceleration and alongside new launches across categories. The company has set up a ‘Unified India’ strategy to streamline organisation and accelerate decision making. Inflation, interest rates, deficient monsoon, are an overhang on consumer demand. It is also aiming at premiumisation. 
 The company has seen downgrades and shares have corrected 20 per cent in the last six months, due to the poor growth outlook and visible macro challenges. The stock could pick up long-term investors’ attention, since it is trading well below its own historical price earnings and enterprise value/Ebitda ranges. The shares gained 2.43 per cent to close at ₹1,857 apiece on Thursday on the BSE.
 According to Bloomberg, 24 of the 32 analysts polled post Q2 were bullish on the stock, two were bearish and six were neutral. Their average one-year target price was ₹2,187 per share. The writer is a New Delhi-based independent journalist

 Reliance Q2 preview: The September quarter performance of Mukesh Ambani-led Reliance Industries (RIL) is expected to be robust, driven primarily by the O2C recovery, with Jio providing steady support. However, Reliance Retail's margins are seen to be under pressure.
 India's most valuable firm, whose telecom arm - Jio Platform - listed on the bourses earlier this week, is slated to post its second quarter results for the ongoing fiscal year (Q2 FY27) on October 30. Along with earnings announcement, the company's board will also consider raising of funds by way via debentures.
 RIL, in line with past quarters, is expected to post its earnings performance post the market trading hours.
 RIL Q2 preview
 Overall, brokerages expect double-digit growth on a yearly basis in topline of the company in the range of 22-30 per cent to ₹3.53 trillion-₹3.09 trillion. The increase in earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) is seen at 11-15 per cent year-on-year (YoY). Meanwhile, profit could see a rise of 15-30 per cent YoY, as per brokerages.
 According to Kotak Institutional Equities (KIE) estimates, the profit is seen rising 30 per cent YoY and 12.8 per cent quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) to ₹23,621.7 crore during the period under review, driven by net sales growth of 38.8 per cent YoY and 14.2 per cent QoQ to ₹3.53 trillion.

docs.title: 6 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Jefferies with 40% to 66% upside
docs.text: From the plane you board to the oil you cook with, Jefferies is betting on several sectors this earnings season. The global investment bank has picked companies that touch everyday life, from insurance and airports to electricity and packaged food. Jefferies kept its 'Buy' ratings on a list of companies with upside potential ranging from 40% to 66%. What could drive these stocks higher, and what should investors watch? Here's what you need to know - CompanyTarget PriceUpsideMax Financial ServicesRs 2,05066%Adani EnterprisesRs 3,83054%JSW EnergyRs 72054%GMR AirportsRs 13551%AWL Agri BusinessRs 26050%Star HealthRs 73040% Jefferies on Max Financial Services: Can growth pick up? Jefferies has maintained a ‘Buy’ rating on Max Financial Services with a target price of Rs 2,050, indicating an upside potential of 66%. According to the global investment bank Jefferies report, the September 2026 quarter’s value of new business (VNB) was in line with estimates. Higher margins offset slower annualised premium equivalent (APE) growth. Jefferies believes concerns about the expense-to-management ratio are overstated and expects a new commission structure, goods and services tax adjustments, and cost savings to reduce the ratio by 7-10 percentage points. ALSO READ2 staffing stocks tapping into India’s $98 billion global capability centre boom Jefferies also sees potential for faster business growth through Axis Bank, where Max Financial has a 65-70% share of insurance sales through the bank. It expects annualised premium equivalent growth to improve in the March 2027 quarter as the comparison base becomes more favourable and new products contribute. Jefferies values the company at 11 times its estimated December 2028 value of new business. Jefferies on Adani Enterprises: Can new businesses sustain growth? Jefferies has a ‘Buy’ rating on Adani Enterprises with a target price of Rs 3,830, implying an upside potential of 54%. The company’s Q2 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) exceeded estimates, supported by airports, copper and other businesses. According to the report, quarterly EBITDA reached Rs 6,320 crore against its estimate of Rs 56 crore. Airport earnings increased 55% year-on-year despite weaker passenger traffic, while the copper business benefited from higher capacity utilisation and by-product prices. Its data centre business also expanded, with contracted capacity crossing 1.2 gigawatts (GW). Jefferies has raised its financial year 2027 EBITDA estimate by around 4%, mainly due to strength in copper.
